edits.fix: Add the id to the footer on all five pages, e.g. "Bellingham Math Circle / Week 7 / K1-1".

edits.quote: It is the other player’s turn. For each move they can make, cross out what they take, then circle what you take to win. [Diagram: two identical copies each of piles 3, 6, 9, with nothing saying which copy is for which reply]
edits.fix: Say that each copy is for a different take, e.g. "Use one picture for each amount they can take." Otherwise a K child crosses out 1 in both copies and never answers the reply of 2. The problem is about answering every reply, so this matters.

edits.quote: Circle what you take to be sure to win, and cross out each trap.
edits.fix: Change to "Circle every take that makes you sure to win." In the {1, 3} game every move from an odd pile wins, and both moves win from 3. That is the surprise in this game, and the singular wording lets a child circle one move and miss it.

edits.quote: Problem 9: Now there is one pile, and each player may take 1 or 3 counters.
edits.fix: Swap pages 4 and 5 so the one-pile rule changes (P6 {1,2,3}, P9 {1,3}, P10 last counter loses) sit together. The two-pile game (P7-P8) then closes the packet as the hardest idea. Adjust the "Now" openings to match.

k-1.summary: A strong, concrete K–1 band. Every pile is drawn, the problems build from traps for {1,2} to answering every reply, the greedy trap (Ben), new rules, two piles with a mirror strategy, and last-counter-loses, and every expected answer checks out. Only small clarity fixes are needed (which copy is which reply in P4, single versus every move in P9), plus a page swap so the one-pile problems stay together.

edits.fix: Add the id to the footer on all five pages, e.g. "Bellingham Math Circle / Week 7 / G23-1".

edits.quote: In every game in this packet, two players take turns taking counters from a pile. Each problem says how many counters a player may take on a turn.
edits.fix: Cut the meta narration: "Two players take turns taking counters. Whoever takes the last counter wins." The "from a pile" wording is also false for P7's two piles.

edits.quote: decide whether you would rather go first or second. Shade the box of every pile where you would rather go second.
edits.fix: Delete the first clause because the shading instruction already says it: "For each starting pile from 1 to 20, shade the box if you would rather go second; otherwise write how many counters you take first."

edits.quote: [Table for piles 30, 50, 61, 100 with only about an inch before Problem 6]
edits.fix: Leave several inches of working space under the table, or move P6 down. Children have to extend the 1-20 pattern of P4 (2, 7, 9, 14, 16, ...) up to 100 and need room to list it.

edits.quote: Find a rule for how many counters a player may take on a turn, so that you would rather go second exactly when the starting pile is 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, and so on. [rest of page blank]
edits.fix: Add three or four blank 1-25 strips, each with a "Rule: ____" line, so children can test candidate rules the way they did in P4 and P6 (answers: {1,2,3,4}, then e.g. {1,2,3,4,6}).

grades-2-3.summary: A well-built 2–3 band. It enters with {1,2}, has children test Lee's and Mo's claims against every reply, classifies {1,3,4}, pushes the pattern to 100, then gives the contrasting parity game, two piles, and an inverse design problem. All answers check out. The edits are small: meta wording in the opening rules, one redundant clause, and missing working space for P5 and P8.

edits.fix: Add the id to the footer on all seven pages, e.g. "Bellingham Math Circle / Week 7 / G45-1".

edits.quote: In every game in this packet, two players take turns taking counters from a pile. Each problem says how many counters a player may take on a turn.
edits.fix: Cut the meta narration: "Two players take turns taking counters. Unless a problem says otherwise, whoever takes the last counter wins."

edits.quote: From now on, a game is named by its list of allowed moves, so the game in Problem 1 is the {1, 3, 4} game. (also P2: "A starting pile where you would rather go second is called a losing pile. Every other starting pile is a winning pile.")
edits.fix: Both are activity-wide definitions used through P10. Move them into the opening rules once, then write P1 as "In the {1, 3, 4} game ..." and drop the definitions from P2 and P3.

edits.quote: When the two piles are the same size, which player can always win? Explain why.
edits.fix: Replace with "Describe the shaded squares and explain why the second player wins from each of them." The equal-piles mirror question is the easy part, already asked of K–1 and 2–3. The grid shows the real 4–5 pattern: second player wins exactly when the piles leave the same remainder on division by 3, e.g. (4,1) and (5,2).

In {2, 3} a pile of 1 has no legal move, and the stated rule ("whoever takes the last counter wins") does not say what happens then, so this example game is undefined. Add "If you cannot move, you lose" to the opening rules, which also covers subsets without 1 in P6, or replace {2, 3} with a game containing 1 such as {1, 4}.

grades-4-5.summary: A deep, well-sequenced 4–5 band. It classifies {1,3,4} and extends it to 2026, compares four rules, tests the greedy plan, proves the pattern continues, finds all four move sets in 1-6 whose losing piles are the multiples of 4, and covers misère, two-pile grids (the {1,3,4} grid gives the non-obvious pairs (1,3), (1,8), (2,7), (3,8), (4,6)), and the pigeonhole argument. All expected answers check out. Fixes are light: the undefined {2,3} example in P10, P8 asking the easy mirror question in place of the grid pattern, and definitions that belong in the opening rules.

overall.strongest: The K–1 band is fully concrete, with drawn piles and 1st/2nd choices, and still covers traps, answering every reply, the greedy mistake, new rules, the two-pile mirror strategy and last-counter-loses, without being watered down.
overall.weakest: The grades 4–5 band has the only real correctness slip: P10 uses the {2,3} game, which is undefined under the stated rules. P8 also asks the easy equal-piles question in place of the full grid pattern.
